title: Blackburn with Darwen staring down £15m black hole as costs spiral
excerpt: The projected shortfall in Blackburn with Darwen Council’s budget has grown to a likely £15m by the end of the decade, it has been revealed.
content:
The projected shortfall in Blackburn with Darwen Council’s budget has grown to a likely £15m by the end of the decade, it has been revealed.

Back in June, forecasts had indicated that this budget black hole would reach £9m by 2029/2030, but spiralling costs now mean that the local authority is staring down a £15m shortfall by this period.

This update to the council’s financial modelling shows that executive members will now have to find £9m to balance the books next year alone, half of which will have to be found from savings, which could mean cuts to services, with the rest coming from an increase to charges, and drawing down £3m from the authority’s reserves.

Presenting the update to the executive board, finance portfolio holder Cllr Vicky McGurk said: "This is the opportunity now for portfolio holders to come up with budget-saving plans in order that we can set the legally required balanced budget."

Finance chief Cllr Vicky McGurk shared the updated forecast at a meeting of the executive board (Image: BWDC)

 Under the council’s ‘worst case’ modelling for the year 2029/2030, this black hole could be as large as £30m, if the cost inflation faced by the authority remains at 8 per cent over the next few years.

The worsening outlook comes despite Blackburn with Darwen ending the last financial year in a comparatively strong position with a slight underspend from the initial forecast.

Yet, everyone is feeling the pinch at the moment due to the sky high energy prices resulting from the wars in Ukraine and Iran, which feed through to almost every part of the economy, from food costs to service provision.

For Blackburn with Darwen, and many councils around the country, these extra costs are being compounded by the ever-increasing price of providing support for the area’s growing number of children with special education needs and disabilities (SEND).

By far the biggest new cost identified by finance officers is an additional £3.6m a year for home-to-school transport, a single budget pressure which accounts for much of the deterioration in the authority's long-term forecasts.

The council has also increased its spending assumptions for concessionary bus fares, winter maintenance and software licensing, while inflation and pay pressures continue to add further costs across a range of services.

The council's 'worst case' scenario sees a £30m budget gap by the end of the decade (Image: Will Morgan)

 At the same time, the council is already forecasting an overspend of almost £2m this year, meaning reserves will need to be used if the position does not improve before the end of March.

The latest forecast paints a picture of an authority facing growing financial pressures despite avoiding some of the crisis situations experienced elsewhere in local government.

But Cllr McGurk insisted the administration would continue trying to protect frontline services where possible.

"We don't want to cut any services," she told the meeting, pointing to how the authority protected libraries and youth centres following more than a decade of cuts from central government. "We have a proud history," the finance chief said.

The report suggests the council remains heavily dependent on reserves to balance future budgets, with the council’s financial back-up sitting at £102m in March.

While much of this is ringfenced to protect wider council services, the portion set aside to protect the authority’s finances is set to take a major hit if additional funding sources or cost savings cannot be found.

Blackburn with Darwen’s Budget Support Reserve stood at just under £14m at the start of the current financial year but is forecast to fall to around £9m by March 2028, if used for this year's overspend and to support next year's budget.

Even increases to Council Tax would not cover the budget gap (Image: Web)

Finance officers warn such reserves are a finite resource and cannot provide a permanent solution to ongoing spending pressures.

The council's financial projections also reveal the scale of uncertainty still facing local authorities.

Under its central forecast, Blackburn with Darwen faces a £15.2m funding gap by 2029/30. However, officials have also modelled a best-case scenario in which the shortfall falls to £3.8m, if these cost pressures decline.

But inflation is not the only issue making it harder to balance the budget each year.

The provision of children's social care continues to be viewed as one of the biggest financial risks facing the authority, while demand for special educational needs support also remains a concern.

During the debate, Executive Member for Children, Young People and Education Cllr Julie Gunn said applications for Education, Health and Care Plans had doubled in the last five years.

The council's Dedicated Schools Grant deficit is now projected to reach more than £33m by 2028 unless government support arrangements continue, with the council expected to fund around 10 per cent of this deficit.

Despite those pressures, Gunn insisted Blackburn with Darwen remained in a stronger position than many authorities.

She said: "Blackburn with Darwen, as you know, has got one of the smallest overspends in SEND on the high-needs budget."

The financial plan will be updated again following this winter's Local Government Finance Settlement, but members were told the current figures mark the start of another difficult budget round as the council attempts to close an almost £9m gap next year while managing a long-term funding shortfall now expected to exceed £15m.

Sharing Blackburn with Darwen’s commitment to keep services running, Cllr McGurk said: "We're a group of sensible people and we do sensible things because we really care about residents.

“That's what being Labour means. We know that we know the value and the cost of what we're doing in adult social care, children's social care, all those things that are statutory, all the things that we talk about.”
